p: Paul opens with the Greek word for a slave, a person owned by a master.
b: Doulos means a slave, someone owned. English "servant" is softer than the word Paul chose. Paul gives himself the title the Old Testament gives to Moses, David and the prophets, "servant" (Hebrew eved) of the LORD, which a Greek reader would hear as "slave." He is claiming honor and ownership at once: he belongs to Christ, and so he speaks with Christ's authority. In Rome many slaves of great households held real power, so the title was not only humble. Paul uses the same picture in 6:16–22, where all people are slaves to someone.
r: Joshua 1:1; Psalm 105:26; Amos 3:7; Galatians 1:10; Philippians 1:1; Titus 1:1; James 1:1; Jude 1:1

a: set apart for the good news of God
p: Paul says God set him apart for a task, as a priest or a prophet is set apart.
b: Aphorizo means to mark off and set aside for a purpose. The Greek Old Testament uses it for offerings and priests set apart for God (Leviticus 20:26; Numbers 8:11). Paul uses it again of his call before birth, in the words of Isaiah 49:1 and Jeremiah 1:5 (Galatians 1:15), and in 15:16 he calls his work "priestly service" for the good news. Some readers hear a pun: the Pharisees' name may come from a Hebrew word meaning "separated" (perushim), and Paul, a former Pharisee, now says he is separated for something else (Philippians 3:5). The pun is a possibility, not something Paul says.
r: Galatians 1:15; Jeremiah 1:5; Isaiah 49:1; Romans 15:16; Philippians 3:5; Acts 13:2

t: "Good news" before the church used the word
p: Rome already used "good news" for announcements about the emperor.
b: Euangelion (our "gospel") is the news a herald brings of victory or a ruler's birth. A calendar inscription from Priene in Asia Minor, set up about 9 BC, calls the birthday of Augustus "the beginning of the good news" for the world. Paul takes a word the empire used for its ruler and fills it with the Bible's own sense: Isaiah's herald who brings good news to Zion, "Your God reigns" (Isaiah 52:7; 40:9; 61:1). Whether Paul meant a pointed contrast with the emperor's gospel is debated. For Roman readers, the contrast would have been hard to miss.

a: through his prophets, in the holy Scriptures
t: The good news was promised in Scripture
p: Paul says his message is not new: the prophets promised it.
b: From the first verse Paul ties the good news to "the holy Scriptures," a phrase found only here in the New Testament. Romans is full of quotations: Paul cites or echoes the Old Testament in nearly every chapter, mostly in the Greek translation (the Septuagint) his readers used. The claim returns at 3:21 ("the Law and the Prophets give witness") and at the very end, in 16:26 ("the writings of the prophets"). For Paul, Jesus does not replace Israel's Scripture but explains it. Readers outside the church ask whether that reading is fair to the original books; see the notes on 4:3 and 3:10–18.

p: Here "flesh" means ordinary human descent, with no blame attached.
b: Paul uses sarx, "flesh," in several ways. Here it means bodily, human descent, as when he calls Abraham "our forefather according to the flesh" (4:1) or speaks of his own people "according to the flesh" (9:3, 5). Elsewhere it means human life that is weak (6:19) or human nature turned against God (7:5; 8:3–13). This site always writes "flesh" and never "sinful nature," so the reader can follow the word through the letter. The pair here, "according to the flesh ... according to the Spirit," sets two stages of the Son's story side by side: born into David's family, then raised in power.

p: The Messiah was to come from David's family.
b: God promised David that a descendant would rule forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 89:3–4), and the prophets spoke of a shoot from Jesse's stump (Isaiah 11:1) and a righteous branch of David (Jeremiah 23:5). Paul uses the Greek Bible's word for "offspring," sperma, the same word used of Abraham's offspring in chapter 4. Matthew and Luke trace Jesus to David through genealogies (Matthew 1:1–17; Luke 3:23–31), and Paul repeats the point at the end of his letter, where he says the root of Jesse rises to rule the nations (15:12). The phrase here may come from a creed older than the letter (see the next note).
r: 2 Samuel 7:12; Psalm 89:3–4; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5; Romans 15:12; Matthew 1:1; 2 Timothy 2:8

a: was marked out as Son of God with power
p: 1:3–4 may be an older creed. Did the resurrection make Jesus Son of God, or show it?
b: Many scholars think 1:3–4 quotes a short confession that Paul's readers already knew: a two-part line about the Son's descent from David and his rank after the resurrection. Marked out (appointed): horizo means to mark out, fix a boundary for, or appoint (Acts 10:42; 17:31), and the Latin Vulgate has praedestinatus, "predestined." Declared: others hear "shown to be." Worry: does this make Jesus Son only at the resurrection (the idea called adoptionism, which the church rejected)? The usual reply is that Paul already calls him God's Son in 1:3 and says God sent his own Son in 8:3. The new thing is the rank "with power," after the resurrection: the Son who was born as a descendant of David is now the ruling Son. Cranfield, Dunn and Fitzmyer differ on details, not on this.

p: This unusual phrase is a Hebrew-style way to say "the Holy Spirit."
b: Elsewhere Paul says "the Holy Spirit" (5:5; 9:1; 14:17; 15:13, 16). Only here does he write "Spirit of holiness," a Hebrew-style phrase like "his holy spirit" in Psalm 51:11 and Isaiah 63:10–11. Readers differ. The Holy Spirit: the same Spirit who raised Jesus (8:11). Christ's own spirit: the holy, divine side of Jesus, set against his human "flesh" in 1:3. The sphere of the age to come: the realm of the Spirit, opposed to the realm of the flesh. The parallel with "flesh" makes the second and third readings possible; the rest of Romans makes the first the common one.

a: by his resurrection from the dead
p: The Greek says "resurrection of dead people," not only "his" resurrection.
b: Literally, "by resurrection of dead ones." Some read this as a general phrase: Jesus' rising is the start of the resurrection of the dead that the Bible's Jewish readers hoped for at the end of the age (Daniel 12:2). Paul states the same idea in 1 Corinthians 15:20, calling Christ "the firstfruits." The preaching in Acts ties Psalm 2:7 to the resurrection (Acts 13:33) and says God made Jesus "Lord and Messiah" through it (Acts 2:36). In Romans the resurrection is the basis of faith (4:24; 10:9) and of the believer's hope (6:4–5; 8:11).
r: Romans 4:24; Romans 10:9; Romans 8:11; Acts 2:36; Acts 13:33; 1 Corinthians 15:20

p: The Greek Bible uses "Lord" in place of God's name, so the title is large.
b: In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, Kyrios, "Lord," stands where the Hebrew has God's own name, YHWH. Paul calls Jesus "Lord" throughout the letter and in 10:9 makes "Jesus is Lord" the confession of faith; in 10:13 he applies to Jesus a verse of Joel about calling on the name of the LORD. The sentence that began with David's family ends with the full title, "Jesus Christ our Lord," so the whole verse moves from earthly descent to the highest title. This site writes "the Lord" (never "the LORD") for Kyrios in the New Testament, even in quotations of the Old.

p: Three readings: obedience that is faith, obedience that comes from faith, or obedience to the faith.
b: Paul frames the letter with this phrase: it returns almost word for word at 16:26. The Greek is a short "obedience of faith," and the "of" can mean three things. Appositional: the obedience that is faith, believing as an act of submitting to the good news (the Catholic Church quotes the phrase in this sense: Dei Verbum 5). Source: obedience that comes from faith, the life that faith produces. Object: obedience to "the faith," the message. Commentators are divided among the three, and all are possible. Dei Verbum quotes the phrase in the first sense; the other two are positions of commentators, not statements of any church; in each, faith and obedience belong together, which matters for the debate over faith and works in 3:20–4:25.

p: The Greek ethne means both "nations" and "non-Jews."
b: Ethne is the Bible's word for the nations of the earth, which in Paul usually means the non-Jewish nations, the Gentiles. The word recalls God's promise to Abraham that all the nations would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3; 18:18), which Paul quotes in a related form in Galatians 3:8. Paul sees himself as sent to the Gentiles (11:13; Galatians 2:7–9), which is why he feels free to write to a church he did not found. Whether most of the Roman believers were Gentiles is debated; see 1:13 and the note on the audience in the introduction.

p: No apostle had founded the Roman church. Paul writes to a group he had not seen.
b: Rome in about AD 56 had perhaps a million people, with a large Jewish community in the district across the Tiber and elsewhere. The believers met in several house gatherings (16:5, 10, 11, 14, 15), not in one hall. No apostle is named as founder; Paul says he does not build on another's foundation (15:20), and Peter's work in Rome is a later tradition. A fourth-century commentator called Ambrosiaster guessed that believing Jews from Rome who had visited Jerusalem started the church. The Roman historian Suetonius (Claudius 25.4) reports that the emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome after riots "at the instigation of Chrestus," and Acts 18:2 mentions Aquila and Priscilla leaving Italy for this reason. Many scholars read that as a quarrel about Christ among Roman Jews. Cassius Dio (Roman History 60.6.6) gives a different, earlier report: under Claudius in AD 41 the Jews were not driven out but forbidden to hold meetings. The two reports may describe two measures or one, and the date of the expulsion is debated.

p: In the Bible "saints" means God's holy people, not a few heroes.
b: Hagioi means "holy ones," people set apart for God. Paul uses it of the ordinary members of a church, as here and in 15:25–31 and 16:2, 15. The Old Testament speaks of Israel as a holy nation (Exodus 19:6) and of "the holy ones of the Most High" who receive the kingdom (Daniel 7:18, 27). Catholic and Orthodox Christians also use "saints" for the honored dead who are with Christ; Protestants usually keep Paul's wider sense. The word in the Greek here does not make that distinction: it names all who are called.

p: Paul joins the Greek greeting "grace" to the Hebrew greeting "peace."
b: The ordinary Greek letter opened with chairein, "greetings." Paul changes it to charis, "grace," and adds the Hebrew shalom as "peace." The greeting thus uses the two languages of the church he is addressing, Jews and Gentiles, and its content is a summary of the letter: God's grace given to people who do not deserve it, and the peace he gives (5:1). Grace, in this site's usage, is the "gift of kindness no one earned." God the Father and the Lord Jesus together are the source of both.
orig: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη (charis hymin kai eirēnē)

a: people are talking about your faith in the whole world
p: Rome's church was known everywhere because Rome was where everyone went.
b: Paul's "all the world" is a figure of speech, but in the capital of the empire news traveled fast: merchants, soldiers, slaves and officials moved between Rome and every province. The Roman historian Tacitus says that by the time of Nero's fire in AD 64 there was a "vast multitude" of Christians in the city (Annals 15.44). Paul's thanks also prepares for a request. He wants to be sent on to Spain from Rome (15:24), and he needs a church that has heard of his message and trusts him.

a: whom I serve with my spirit
p: The verb Paul uses is the one for priestly and temple service.
b: Latreuo means to serve God, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the worship offered in the tabernacle and temple. Paul uses it of his own service, "in my spirit," meaning from the center of his person, and "in the good news of his Son." Telling the good news is his form of worship. In 12:1 he will ask the Romans to offer their bodies as a "sacrifice" in their own worship, and in 15:16 he calls his mission "priestly service." The three passages together show how he thinks of worship: a whole life, not an hour in a building.

p: Paul wanted to reach Rome. He arrived as a prisoner.
b: Paul's prayer to reach Rome is answered in a way he did not expect. After the collection trip to Jerusalem (15:25–31) he was arrested, and Acts tells how he arrived in Rome under guard. When Paul came, the brothers in Rome walked out to meet him: "Word about us had reached the brothers from there, and they came out to meet us at Appius' Market and at Three Taverns" (Acts 28:15). Acts 28:16 adds: "Once we had entered Rome, Paul was given permission to stay on his own, along with the soldier assigned to guard him." Whether the Romans paid for his journey to Spain (15:24) is not known from Acts.

p: Paul does not say which gift. He means something the Spirit gives for strengthening.
b: Charisma pneumatikon is a gift from the Spirit. Paul does not explain it here. He cannot mean a miracle he alone performs, since he goes on in 1:12 to say that he will also be strengthened by their faith. Most readers think he means the teaching in this letter itself, or his way of helping them understand the good news. In 12:6–8 he lists gifts given to every church member. The word is related to charis, "grace," so a gift is something given freely, not earned.

p: The Greek adelphoi is a plural "brothers" that includes women.
b: Adelphoi is the masculine plural of "brother." The Greek plural is also used of a group that includes women, and Acts shows it: Luke uses it of the mixed gathering of the believers in Jerusalem (Acts 1:15, where Mary and the women are among those present, Acts 1:14), of the Christians Paul meets in Jerusalem (Acts 21:17) and of the believers at Puteoli (Acts 28:14). Whether Paul means men only or the whole church is settled by the letter itself: he writes to a church in which Phoebe, Prisca, Junia and other women are greeted by name (16:1, 3, 7). This site follows the form used in Acts and writes "brothers" in the Plain, with a gloss giving "brothers and sisters." A church today would say "brothers and sisters," and the gloss supplies that.
r: Romans 16:1; Romans 16:3; Romans 16:7; Acts 1:14; Acts 1:15; Acts 21:17; Acts 28:14

p: Greeks called anyone who did not speak Greek a "barbarian." Paul says he owes both groups.
b: Barbaros imitates the sound "bar-bar" and was the Greek name for people who spoke other languages. The Romans, who spoke Latin, were barbarians in Greek eyes, though many educated Romans spoke Greek. By pairing "Greeks and barbarians" with "the wise and the foolish," Paul covers every kind of person. In his writing "Jews and Greeks" often means Jews and non-Jews (3:9; 10:12), but here "Greeks and barbarians" is a division inside the Gentile world. His debt is the debt of a messenger who holds a gift for others (15:27).

p: The "Romans debate": a summary of the gospel, a base for Spain, or a plea for unity?
b: Paul is eager to preach to believers who already have the good news. Why? A summary of his gospel (Bornkamm's "last will and testament"). A base for Spain: he needs Rome's support for the mission west (15:24; Jewett). Unity of Jew and Gentile house churches after the return of Jews who were exiled under Claudius, with the weak and the strong (chapters 14–15; Wedderburn, Stowers, Wright). A defense before Jerusalem: he is rehearsing the arguments he must make to Jewish Christians before he delivers the collection (Jervell). Most scholars combine two or three of these. The introduction gives the full list.

p: In a world of honor and shame, a crucified Messiah was a hard thing to be proud of.
b: Rome ranked people by honor. A message about a king executed by Rome on a cross would sound foolish and shameful (1 Corinthians 1:18–25). Paul answers with the understated "I am not ashamed." The Old Testament often prays that those who trust God not be put to shame (Psalm 25:2–3), and Paul will quote Isaiah's promise in 9:33 and 10:11 that the one who trusts in the stone will not be put to shame. For Paul, the cross is God's power, not his weakness. The sentence also announces the theme of the letter in the next verse.
r: Psalm 25:2; Isaiah 28:16; Romans 9:33; Romans 10:11; 1 Corinthians 1:18; 2 Timothy 1:8

p: In Romans "salvation" is mostly still to come: rescue from God's anger on the last day.
b: Soteria means rescue or safety, and also health. In Romans it is mostly future: believers will be saved from the coming anger (5:9–10), and salvation is nearer now than when they first believed (13:11). Paul can also say believers were saved in hope (8:24). The tension between what is already true and what is still coming runs through the letter. Christians have disagreed on whether salvation can be lost and how certain it is (see the card on 8:31–39, written by another part). The power at work is God's, not the power of the speaker or of the law.

p: "First" marks the order in God's plan, not a rank among people.
b: Paul says the good news comes "first for the Jew and for the Greek as well" (the Greek here means non-Jew; see 3:9). It repeats in 2:9–10, where judgment and reward come to the Jew first. The order is historical, not a ranking: the promises were given to Israel (3:1–2; 9:4–5) and the Messiah came from Israel (9:5). Acts shows the same order in Paul's practice, going first to the synagogue (Acts 13:46; 17:2). Later Christian readers sometimes used the phrase to say that Jews had their chance and lost it. Paul says the opposite in chapter 11, where he insists that God has not rejected his people (11:1; see the other parts).

p: A gift from God, God's own justice, his covenant faithfulness, or his saving power?
b: Dikaiosyne theou is the key phrase of Romans (1:17; 3:5, 21, 22, 25, 26; 10:3). Readers have taken it four ways. A gift: the right standing God gives to those who believe (Luther's discovery, in the tower, that God's righteousness is something he gives, not something that condemns). God's own justice: his character, which punishes sin and rewards good (the older Latin reading Luther first feared). Covenant faithfulness: God doing what he promised to Abraham (Wright, Hays). Saving power: God's action that rescues the world (Käsemann). The Old Testament uses "the LORD's righteous acts" for his saving deeds (Judges 5:11; Psalm 98:2). The senses may overlap, and the Plain keeps "God's righteousness" so the reader can follow the word.
r: Romans 3:5; Romans 3:21–26; Romans 10:3; Judges 5:11; Psalm 98:2; Isaiah 51:5

p: A puzzling phrase with many readings; most agree it stresses faith alone.
b: The Greek is a short ek pisteos eis pistin. Readings: from Christ's or God's faithfulness to human faith (Hays); from the faith of the Old Testament to faith in the gospel (some church fathers); from one stage of faith to a deeper one (Calvin); "by faith from start to finish," or "entirely by faith" (the sense in many modern English versions and in Moo). The Plain keeps the Greek words so the reader sees them. All the readings agree that the way God's righteousness is received is faith, and not works.
orig: ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν (ek pisteos eis pistin)

a: The righteous will live by faith.
p: Paul quotes Habakkuk's motto. The Hebrew, the Greek and Paul each differ a little.
b: The Hebrew of Habakkuk 2:4 says the righteous person will live "by his faithfulness" (be'emunato), set against the proud Babylonian. The Greek Old Testament mostly reads "by my faithfulness" (God's), and Codex Alexandrinus moves the "my" to "my righteous one." Paul writes neither "my" nor "his": "by faith." Hebrews 10:38 and Galatians 3:11 also quote the verse. The Qumran commentary on Habakkuk (1QpHab 8) applies the verse to those who keep the Torah and have faith in the Teacher of Righteousness. The Talmud (Makkot 24a) says Habakkuk reduced all the commandments to this one. The Greek can be read two ways: "the one who is righteous by faith will live" or "the righteous will live by faith." Interpreters have defended both; Cranfield and Barth chose the first.
orig: ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται (ho de dikaios ek pisteōs zēsetai)

p: Is "anger" a feeling, a process, or the last judgment? Paul uses it of all three.
b: The Greek orge ("anger," the word this site uses for God's wrath) is "revealed" in the same breath as God's righteousness (1:17). The next verses show what Paul means: God "handed them over" to what they chose (1:24, 26, 28). Readings: an impersonal process in which sin brings its own damage (C. H. Dodd); God's personal opposition to evil, steady and not like human temper (Cranfield, Morris, Stott); the day of anger still to come (2:5, 8; 5:9). Marcion, who thought anger belonged to the creator-God and not to the Father of Jesus, found verses like this one hard to keep. See the topic on God's wrath.

a: What can be known about God is plain among them
t: Can people know God from creation?
p: Paul says God makes himself known through what he made. The churches disagree on how far this goes.
b: Paul's point is that no one can claim to have had no chance to know (1:20). The Old Testament says the heavens tell God's glory (Psalm 19:1–4) and Acts shows Paul using the idea in Lystra and Athens (Acts 14:15–17; 17:22–31). The churches disagree on what this knowledge can do: it can lead to God (Catholic teaching since the Council of Vatican I), or it only leaves people without excuse (Reformed), or it is cancelled by sin (Barth). See the card below for the churches' positions. The key word is "plain" (phaneron), which Paul uses again in 3:21 for what God did in Christ.
r: Psalm 19:1–4; Acts 14:15–17; Acts 17:22–31; Romans 2:14–15; Wisdom of Solomon 13:1–9

a: his everlasting power and divine nature
p: A Jewish book from before Paul argues much the same, then blames the nations for idolatry.
b: The Wisdom of Solomon (a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians count as Scripture; Protestants do not) argues in 13:1–9 that people should have found the Maker from the beauty of what he made. It says that the nature-worshipers are not to be excused, because they stopped at the creation (Wisdom of Solomon 13:8). Paul's argument in 1:19–25 follows that pattern step by step, and 14:22–27 of the same book lists the vices that follow idolatry, as Paul does in 1:29–31. The resemblance suggests Paul is using a way of arguing familiar in Jewish synagogues about Gentiles. The Greek philosophers, the Stoics above all, argued for God from the order of the world; the Jewish writers borrowed the argument and aimed it at idolatry.
orig: ἥ τε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης (hē aidios autou dynamis kai theiotēs)
r: Wisdom of Solomon 13:1–9; Wisdom of Solomon 14:22–27; Psalm 19:1; Acts 17:24–29

p: The same Greek word appears again in 2:1. Paul uses it to link two accusations.
b: Anapologetos means "without a defense" and is the root of the English "apologetics." Paul uses it here for people who suppress what God has shown and again in 2:1 for the person who judges them. The repetition ties the two paragraphs together: the person who agreed with the verdict in 1:18–32 is the person who stands in the dock in 2:1. The word is rare in the New Testament; here it is not a technical claim that no one can ever be saved, only that no one can defend the choice to ignore God.

a: They traded the glory of the immortal God for a likeness
t: Israel's golden calf behind the Gentile picture
p: Paul's words echo the Bible's story of Israel and the calf, and also Adam.
b: Psalm 106:20 says Israel "traded their glory for the shape of an ox that feeds on grass." Paul's wording is close to the Greek Psalm: "they exchanged their glory for a likeness of a calf." Jeremiah 2:11 says the same: my people have swapped their glory. The animals Paul lists, birds, four-footed animals and crawling things, also recall the creatures of Genesis 1:20–26, which Adam and Eve were set above. Richard Hays and others argue that 1:18–32 describes humanity's fall in the language of Adam and of Israel's idolatry, so that the reader who hears "they" as "the Gentiles" will find at 2:1 and 2:17 that the story has also been about Israel. Paul never says so outright.

p: God hands humanity over in 1:24, 26 and 28. The same verb is used of the cross.
b: Paradidomi appears at 1:24, 26 and 28: God "handed them over" to impurity, to shameful passions, and to a mind that fails the test. The picture is of a judge who lets people take what they chose, not one who forces them. Each handing-over follows the sin it answers (swapping glory, truth, knowledge). The same verb is used of Jesus: God handed his own Son over for us all (8:32), and Jesus "was handed over for our trespasses" (4:25; compare Isaiah 53:12). Readers who see the link say that the cross is God entering the very situation that he hands humanity over to.
r: Romans 1:26; Romans 1:28; Romans 4:25; Romans 8:32; Isaiah 53:12; Psalm 81:12

t: A blessing in the middle of an accusation
p: Paul breaks into praise, as a Jewish speaker would after mentioning idols.
b: In the middle of a charge against the nations Paul adds a blessing of the Creator, as Jewish writers did when naming something shocking (compare 9:5; 2 Corinthians 11:31). It reminds the reader that the One who is wronged is also the One "blessed forever"; the accusation never turns Paul's own eyes from God. "The lie" (pseudos) is a Bible word for idols: Jeremiah 10:14 calls images "a lie," and Isaiah 44:20 asks if the idol is not "a lie" in the maker's hand. Paul's readers would have recognized the charge as a standard Jewish criticism of pagan worship.

p: "Nature" here means the way things are meant to be, a Greek and Jewish idea.
b: Physis, "nature," appears in Romans at 1:26; 2:14, 27; 11:21, 24. Greek and Roman writers spoke of acts "against nature," and Jewish writers such as Philo (Special Laws 3.37–42) and Josephus (Against Apion 2.199) used the same idea to condemn same-sex acts. Paul's wording "natural use" (chresis) treats sexual relations as a use of the body; the Greek does not say "of their bodies," and the Plain does not add it. At 1:27 the same phrase is "the natural use of the woman." Readers differ on what Paul meant by "nature": an order built into creation (Gagnon, Hays, and most church teaching), or the custom and social order of his day (Boswell; for a different path, Stowers on self-mastery). The Plain keeps the Greek words so the reader sees what they say.
r: Romans 2:14; Romans 2:27; Romans 11:24; Leviticus 18:22; Leviticus 20:13; 1 Corinthians 11:14

p: This is the only place in the Bible that may speak of sex between women.
b: Paul does not use the words "lesbian" or "women with women" here; he says "their women changed the natural use for one against nature." Many modern readers (Brooten, Hays) take this to mean sex between women, and Chrysostom (Homilies on Romans 4) reads it that way. Some earlier readers took it to mean unnatural acts between a woman and a man, and the Greek does allow that; Augustine, writing on marriage, applied the language of use "against nature" to intercourse that departs from its natural purpose, even between husband and wife. Brooten argues that Paul and his world treated female-female sex as a break in the proper order of the sexes. Whatever 1:26 means, it is placed before 1:27 as part of a single list, and the point is the exchange of what is natural, not a separate teaching.

a: Men did shameful things with men
t: How the churches and scholars read 1:26–27
p: The churches teach different things, and scholars read the verses at least three ways.
b: All same-sex acts are wrong. Paul draws on Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 and the Jewish view of nature; this is the teaching of Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches (Gagnon; Hays, who also calls the church to welcome people). The verses condemn something narrower: pederasty, exploitation, excess or temple prostitution in the Roman world (Boswell, Countryman); the Bible has no word for sexual orientation. A rhetorical setup: Paul describes pagan excess to bring a moral reader into agreement before turning on that reader in 2:1 (Stowers, Hays). Churches that hold the first view differ on how to treat people; others have reconsidered. See the card below, and the full topic page.

p: Paul says the act brings its own result. He does not say what the result is.
b: Antimisthia is a payment in return, wages. The "error" (plane) is the wandering of idolatry in 1:23–25, not only the sexual act. Readers disagree on what the payment is: the dishonor of 1:24 itself, the loss of self-mastery, the harm of the practices, or the final judgment of 2:5. The older church fathers often read the payment as the shame and loss of dignity in the act. Because the sentence is tied back to idolatry, many readers say the main point is that worship of what is made leads to lives that are less than human.

a: a mind that fails the test
p: Paul puns on two forms of the Greek word for "approve after testing."
b: The people "did not think it worth" (edokimasan, literally "did not test and approve") keeping God in their knowledge, so God handed them over to an adokimon mind, a mind that is tested and rejected, a counterfeit coin or failed metal. The same root appears in 2:18 ("you can test what matters") and 12:2, where Paul speaks of testing the will of God. The Plain keeps the pun as best it can. Translations usually say "depraved" or "debased" mind, which loses the link to testing.

a: Every kind of unrighteousness, wickedness, greed and evil
p: Greek and Jewish writers made lists of vices. Paul's has 21 items.
b: Lists of vices were a common tool in Greek philosophy and in Jewish teaching: see Wisdom of Solomon 14:22–27 for a Jewish list that sets out the results of idolatry; Paul gives others in 1 Corinthians 5:10–11, 6:9–10 and Galatians 5:19–21. Some of Paul's words are paired by sound in Greek, which helps memory. Sexual sin is not named in the earliest manuscripts' list here (the Byzantine text adds "sexual immorality"), because 1:24–27 has just spoken of it. The list reaches ordinary faults, gossip and disobedience to parents, so that every reader finds himself on it.
r: Wisdom of Solomon 14:22–27; 1 Corinthians 5:10–11; Galatians 5:19–21; Colossians 3:5–8

p: The Greek can mean either; it appears nowhere else in the New Testament.
b: Theostygeis is rare. It can be active, "haters of God," or passive, "hated by God" or "hateful to God." Most English translations and many commentators take the active sense, in line with 1:21 (people who did not honor God); the passive sense, "hated by God," is also possible. The Plain follows the active reading. Either way, the list is of those who set themselves against God.

p: The Greek asynthetoi recalls the prophets' charge against faithless Judah.
b: Asynthetos means someone who does not keep an agreement. The Greek Old Testament uses it for "faithless Judah" in Jeremiah 3:7–11, where Judah is called treacherous for breaking the covenant with God. The alert reader who has heard Jeremiah's charge will notice, perhaps, that Paul's list of Gentile vices contains a word the prophets used of Israel. The ending of the list, "no family love ... no mercy," also names the failure of the kindness the next chapter will say God shows (2:4).

p: Paul says everyone knows that such acts deserve death, yet applauds them.
b: Dikaioma is a righteous ruling or requirement. It will return in 2:26, where an uncircumcised person keeps the law's "requirements." The Gentiles "know" God's ruling, which prepares for the claim in 2:14–15 that the law's work is written on their hearts. "Death" here is more than the biological end: in Paul sin leads to death (5:12; 6:23). The final charge, that people applaud those who do such things, shows the worst form of the problem: moral knowledge that is silenced by shared habit. It leads straight into 2:1, where the person who judges others is told they do the same.

p: Paul speaks to a judge. Scholars disagree on whether he means a Gentile, a Jew, or any reader.
b: Paul turns suddenly from "they" (1:18–32) to a single "you" who judges. This is the style of the ancient diatribe, a lecture with an imaginary partner who is answered and corrected (the Greek Stoic Epictetus teaches this way). Who is the partner? A Gentile moralist who agrees with Paul's list of vices (Stowers). A Jew from the start, since only a Jew would judge by God's law (Dunn, Wright, Moo; the "you" is named a Jew at 2:17). Anyone who agrees with 1:18–32, Jew or Gentile, a reader whom Paul does not yet name. A trap of this kind has a Bible model: Nathan's story told to David, who judges it and is told, "You are the man" (2 Samuel 12:1–7). The Wisdom of Solomon (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians) has a similar turn: after condemning the idol-makers of the nations, chapter 15 begins by saying that our God is kind and slow to anger, and that "we" belong to him, which can sound like comfort and can be taken as complacency.
r: 2 Samuel 12:1–7; Wisdom of Solomon 15:1–4; Romans 2:17; Romans 3:9

a: his kindness, his forbearance and his patience
p: These three words echo Exodus 34:6 and the Jewish prayer that God delays judgment so people can repent.
b: The Old Testament says God is "slow to anger," kind and faithful (Exodus 34:6; Psalm 103:8), and the Wisdom of Solomon (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians) teaches that God overlooks sins to give people time to repent (Wisdom of Solomon 11:23; 12:10). Paul uses the same idea against someone who takes God's delay as approval. "Forbearance" (anoche) returns at 3:25, where God's earlier patience with sins is part of the reason Christ's death was needed. The delay is meant to lead to repentance, and 2 Peter 3:9 says the same.
r: Exodus 34:6; Psalm 103:8; Wisdom of Solomon 11:23; Romans 3:25; 2 Peter 3:9

p: Paul uses a money word: the person who despises God's riches (2:4) is saving up anger as a treasure.
b: The verb thesaurizo means to store treasure. Paul sets two treasures side by side: the "riches" of God's kindness (2:4) and the store of anger that a hard heart builds up. The "day of anger" is the Old Testament "day of the LORD" as a day of judgment (Zephaniah 1:15; Isaiah 13:9). Jesus uses a similar picture of storing up treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:19–21). The line prepares for the great reversal of the letter: the same God whose anger is stored up is the one who in Christ gives grace (5:20–21).

p: Paul quotes a standard Old Testament idea. How does it fit with "not by works" in 3:20?
b: "He will pay back each person according to his works" echoes Psalm 62:12, Proverbs 24:12 and Job 34:11: "you pay each person back by what he does" (Psalm 62:12). Jesus says it (Matthew 16:27) and so does Paul elsewhere (2 Corinthians 5:10). Yet in 3:20, 28 he says no one is justified by works. Readings: Paul is describing the standard of the final judgment, which the gospel has not removed, and which a believer meets by Spirit-given obedience (Wright, Cranfield); he describes the standard that people in fact fail (Luther); this is common ground with the synagogue, whose teaching Paul shares here (Sanders, Donfried); or he speaks of what Christians achieve by grace-enabled merit (Catholic teaching). See the card on 2:6–11.
r: Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12; Job 34:11; Jeremiah 17:10; Matthew 16:27; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Revelation 20:12

p: Paul says the Jew comes first in reward and in judgment: the one given more is held to more.
b: In 1:16 "the Jew first" meant first to hear the good news. Here the same words apply to trouble and glory alike (2:9, 10). It fits a basic biblical idea: those who were given the law are held to a higher account (Amos 3:2: God says that because he knew Israel alone of all the clans of the earth, he will hold it to account for all its crimes). Paul adds that God shows no favorites (2:11): being first is not a free pass. This is the setup for 3:1–9, where he asks what advantage the Jew has.

p: A Greek word built from the Hebrew phrase "lift the face."
b: Prosopolempsia was probably coined by Jewish Greek speakers from the Hebrew idiom nasa panim, "to lift the face," meaning to favor someone because of who they are. The Bible repeatedly says God does not do this: "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17; compare 2 Chronicles 19:7; Sirach 35:12–15, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians count as Scripture). Peter learns it at Cornelius' house (Acts 10:34). The sentence is the hinge of the paragraph: if God judges without favorites, then having the law cannot protect the Jew, and lacking it cannot excuse the Gentile.

a: Those who sinned without the law
p: Paul divides humanity into those who have the Torah and those who do not. Jewish teachers did too.
b: "Without the law" means without the Torah of Moses, that is, Gentiles. Jewish teaching held that God still held non-Jews accountable: the rabbis later spoke of seven laws given to Noah's descendants (the "Noahide" laws, see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 56a–b), and many taught that righteous Gentiles have a share in the world to come. Paul agrees that the nations are accountable (1:20), and goes on to say that they show "what the law contains" in their conscience (2:14–15). The word "perish" in this verse (apollymi) means destruction, not only dying.

p: A court word: to be declared in the right. Is it a verdict, or a making right?
b: Dikaioo comes from a word for "right" and belongs to the law court: a judge justifies a person when he declares that person in the right (the Hebrew hitsdiq; Deuteronomy 25:1). Here Paul means the verdict of the last day. He says elsewhere the verdict is already given to those who trust in Christ (3:24; 5:1, 9). The churches have read the word differently since the Reformation. Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 7) says that justification is not only the forgiveness of sins but also the sanctification and renewal of the inner person, and Latin iustificare was understood as "to make just"; the Reformers said the word is about a verdict, with holiness following. See the card at 3:21–31 for the churches' positions.

a: do by nature what the law contains
t: Gentiles who do what the law says
p: Who are these Gentiles: non-Christians with a moral sense, or Gentile Christians?
b: Paul says Gentiles "do by nature what the law contains." Non-Christian Gentiles who follow their moral sense: Chrysostom, Pelagius, Aquinas, Calvin (who adds that this does not save them), Moo, Fitzmyer. Gentile Christians in whom the Spirit writes the law, as Jeremiah 31:33 promised: the later Augustine (On the Spirit and the Letter), Barth, Cranfield, and Wright. The Greek "by nature" can go with "do" or with "do not have the law" (Gentiles who by nature lack it). The Greek and Roman Stoics spoke of a natural law written in every human being, an idea the Jewish teacher Philo had already applied to Moses' law. See the card on natural revelation at 1:19–20 for how the churches use this.

p: This is the language of the promised new covenant. Paul applies it to Gentiles.
b: Jeremiah promised a new covenant in which God says, "I will put my law inside them, and on their hearts I will write it" (Jeremiah 31:33). Ezekiel promised a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Paul says the same of Gentiles who do what the law contains: its "work" is written on their hearts. If he means Gentile Christians, the sentence describes the new covenant at work (Wright, Cranfield); if he means all people, it describes a witness every conscience bears, something short of the new covenant (Moo). In 2 Corinthians 3:3 he calls the Corinthians a letter written by the Spirit of the living God on human hearts, not in ink on stone.

p: Paul's word syneidesis was a Greek term. Hebrew had no single word for it.
b: Syneidesis, literally "knowing together with oneself," is a Greek word for the inner witness of a person's own deeds. The Hebrew Bible speaks of the "heart" (lev) that strikes or reproaches a person (1 Samuel 24:5; Job 27:6), and the word syneidesis is rare in the Greek Old Testament, with Ecclesiastes 10:20 and Wisdom of Solomon 17:10 as clear cases. Paul uses it in Romans of what bears witness in Gentiles (2:15), in himself (9:1) and in the case of obeying authorities (13:5). Here the conscience testifies and the thoughts argue for and against, like a trial in the mind.

t: "According to my good news" and the theory of an added line
p: A few scholars think 2:16 was added later. Most defend it; "my" good news is Paul's usual way of speaking.
b: Paul says the judgment is "through Christ Jesus," and "according to my good news." The idea that God judges through Christ is found in Acts 17:31 and in 2 Corinthians 5:10. A few scholars (Bultmann first; others since) argued that 2:16 interrupts the thought between 2:15 and 2:17 and was added by a later editor; some move it. The great majority defend the verse as Paul's, pointing to "my good news" in 16:25 and to the fact that the standard editions report no manuscript without it. Paul's "my" good news does not mean a private message but the message he was called to preach (1:1).

t: "A Jew" and the praise of Judah
p: The name "Jew" comes from Judah, whose name means "praise." Paul plays on this in 2:29.
b: The word Ioudaios comes from Judah, the son whose name Leah chose from the Hebrew for "praise": "This time I will praise the LORD" (Genesis 29:35). Paul's "praise" in 2:29 puns on the name. Here the speaker is the Jew in the diatribe, whose pride rests on the law and on God. The Old Testament itself both honors this pride and warns against it (Jeremiah 9:23–24; Psalm 50:16–21). Jewish readers have asked whether Paul's picture of Jewish teachers who steal and commit adultery fits real Jewish practice; most modern scholars say it is a rhetorical type, not a description of all Jews.

a: the very form of knowledge and truth
p: Morphosis can mean the outline, the embodiment, or only the outward form.
b: Morphosis is a rare word. It can mean the genuine shape or embodiment of something (the law as the very body of knowledge and truth), or only a form or outline without the substance (as in 2 Timothy 3:5, "having a form of godliness"). The first reading makes Paul affirm the law's value; the second, to doubt its holder's use of it. The context favors the first: the speaker is confident that the law gives him the real thing, and Paul does not say the law is empty but that its possessors fail to live by it (2:21–23).

p: Stealing and adultery are from the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:14–15).
b: Paul takes two of the Ten Words, "You must not steal" and "You must not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:15, 14; Deuteronomy 5:17–19), and a charge concerning idols from the first table (Exodus 20:3–6). In Hebrew the order is murder, adultery, stealing; the Greek Old Testament varies it, and Paul's order, stealing and adultery, differs. The point is the same: the teacher who preaches the law while breaking it. Paul does not say that the person addressed actually steals; the questions are rhetorical, as the diatribe's questions are. Jesus makes a similar charge against teachers who say and do not do (Matthew 23:3).

p: The charge is unclear. Jews were forbidden to plunder idol temples, so Paul may mean something else.
b: Hierosyleo is "to rob a temple." The Torah forbids taking the gold of idols (Deuteronomy 7:25) and Josephus says Jewish law forbids robbing the temples of other peoples (Antiquities 4.207); in Acts 19:37 the Ephesian town clerk says Paul's companions are "not temple robbers." Readings: some Jews did plunder or deal in idols' goods; the charge is a figure for using what belongs to God, such as withholding tithes (Malachi 3:8); or an allusion to the scandal reported by Josephus in which Jewish swindlers took money meant for the Jerusalem temple from a Roman noblewoman, Fulvia, which led to the expulsion of Jews from Rome under Tiberius (Antiquities 18.81–84). That last proposal is not certain, but it would make the charge fit a Roman audience.

a: The name of God is insulted among the Gentiles because of you.
p: Paul's Greek is closer to the Greek Isaiah than to the Hebrew.
b: Paul quotes Isaiah 52:5. This site's Plain of the Hebrew reads: "my name is treated with contempt" (Isaiah 52:5). The Greek Old Testament adds "because of you" and "among the Gentiles," which Paul uses. In Isaiah the nations scorn God's name because Israel is in exile; Paul reads it as a result of the failure of the people who carry God's name (2:23). In some Jewish thought, profaning the Name through bad behavior, and the opposite, "sanctifying the Name," were central ethical ideas. Ezekiel 36:20–23 says the same of Israel in exile.

t: Circumcision is real, and not a free pass
p: Paul agrees that circumcision means something. The prophets also warned that it was not enough.
b: Circumcision was God's command to Abraham as the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17:10–14). Paul says it "is of value," with a condition: that one keep the law. The prophets said the same before him: the command to "circumcise the foreskin of your heart" (Deuteronomy 10:16), Jeremiah declared that Israel and the nations alike are "uncircumcised in heart" (Jeremiah 9:25–26), and Moses promised that God would one day circumcise their hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6). So Paul speaks as a Jewish teacher, not against his people but with the prophets. Roman writers such as Tacitus mocked circumcision as a mark of Jewish separateness (Histories 5.5).
r: Genesis 17:10–14; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4; Jeremiah 9:25–26; Romans 3:1–2

p: "Letter" means the written code of the law. It is not Paul's word for a lifeless reading.
b: Gramma means a written letter or document. Paul sets "letter" against "spirit" in 2:29, in 7:6 and in 2 Corinthians 3:6, where serving in the new way of the Spirit is set against serving in the old way of the written code. He does not mean that the law is lifeless or that a literal reading is wrong: he says in 7:12 that the law is holy. He means that a law that stands outside a person, even with the sign of circumcision, cannot by itself change the heart. The new covenant of Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36 is what changes it.

a: is not a Jew who is one on the outside
p: Paul seems to redefine "Jew." Jewish readers hear it differently from later Christians.
b: Does Paul take the name "Jew" away from the physical people of Israel? Supersessionist reading: the church is the true Israel and the outward Jew has lost the name (a reading used in Christian history to justify contempt for Jews). The prophets' own argument: Paul, like Jeremiah and Moses, says a Jew must have a circumcised heart; he is calling Jews to be what they are (Moo, Dunn). Paul among Jews: he is speaking to Gentile believers, or to a Gentile who thinks of himself as a Jew, not about Jews generally (Nanos, Stowers, Fredriksen). Daniel Boyarin argues that Paul's inner-outer pattern resembles Platonizing Jewish thought and that Rabbinic Judaism chose the opposite emphasis on the body and descent. In 3:1–2 and 11:1 Paul insists that the Jews' advantage has not ended.

p: Paul ends with a pun on the name of Judah, which means "praise."
b: "Jew" (Ioudaios) comes from Judah (Yehudah), "praise" (Genesis 29:35; 49:8). In Paul's line, the real Jew is one whose "praise," epainos, comes from God. Jewish readers will recognize the play, which works in Hebrew and is only suggested in Greek. Paul's standard is not a rejection of Jewish identity: he takes pride in the name himself and later says that he too is an Israelite (11:1). "In spirit" may mean the human spirit (the inner person) or the Holy Spirit (as in 7:6 and 8:4). The Plain keeps the neutral "in spirit."

p: After 2:25–29 a Jewish listener would ask: is there any point in being a Jew? Paul says yes.
b: Paul has just said that circumcision counts for nothing without obedience (2:25–29). A Jewish reader would ask what is left of Israel's privilege. Paul's first answer is "Much, in every way" and he does not take it back: in 9:4–5 he lists the gifts again, and in 11:1 he insists that God has not rejected his people. Stendahl argued that Romans is not about how a lonely sinner finds peace but about how Jews and Gentiles belong together in God's plan; the question here is the Jew's place in that plan. The questions that follow (3:1–8) are the objections of an imagined Jewish partner, answered by Paul.

p: Does Paul mean the Scriptures, the promises, or both?
b: Logia are "sayings" or "oracles," words that come from God. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the LORD's words (Psalm 12:6; Numbers 24:4, 16), and Acts 7:38 calls the law given at Sinai "living oracles." Readings: the whole written Scripture (Josephus, Against Apion 1.38–42, says the Jews guard their sacred books with care); the promises made to Israel (Moo, Dunn); or the commands and the promises together. The Greek verb "entrusted" shows that Israel has been given the oracles as a trust, not as a possession: it must keep them for the world.
orig: τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ (ta logia tou theou)

p: The Greek word pistis, usually "faith," here means God's own faithfulness to his promise.
b: Pistis means trust or faith; it can also mean faithfulness. Here the verbs play on it: "disbelieved" (epistesan), "unbelief" (apistia) and "God's faithfulness" (pistin tou theou), a Hebrew-style idea of God's steadfast keeping of his word (emunah; Psalm 89:1–2). Some scholars add that because Paul can use pistis for a faithfulness here, "the pistis of Jesus Christ" in 3:22 and 26 may also mean a faithfulness, Christ's own. That is one proposal among others, and the question there is a different one (see the note at 3:22). The question of 3:3 is the first form of the letter's great concern in chapters 9–11: whether Israel's failure cancels God's promise.
orig: τὴν πίστιν τοῦ θεοῦ (tēn pistin tou theou)

p: Paul's strong denial, used ten times in Romans.
b: Me genoito, literally "may it not happen," is Paul's strongest denial. He uses it ten times in Romans (3:4, 6, 31; 6:2, 15; 7:7, 13; 9:14; 11:1, 11). Elsewhere in his letters it appears in 1 Corinthians 6:15 and in Galatians (2:17; 3:21; 6:14), and once in Luke 20:16. It belongs to the diatribe: the teacher raises an objection in the mouth of an imagined partner and rejects it in one word before he explains. The Greek Stoic Epictetus uses the same phrase in the same way. The KJV renders it "God forbid." This site writes "By no means!" each time, so the reader can see the pattern.
r: Romans 3:6; Romans 3:31; Romans 6:2; Romans 9:14; Romans 11:1; Galatians 2:17

a: So that you may be proved right in your words, and win your case when you are judged.
p: Paul follows the Greek Psalm, which says "when you are judged." The Hebrew says "when you judge."
b: Paul quotes David's prayer of repentance. This site's Plain of the Hebrew reads: "So you are in the right when you speak, / and clear when you pass judgment" (Psalm 51:4). The Greek Psalm says God will win "when you are judged" (passive), which Paul keeps. The Greek picture is of God put on trial by human unfaithfulness; the verdict will vindicate him. In the Psalm, David confesses his sin against Bathsheba and Uriah and says God's verdict is just. Paul makes the confession a pattern: human sin cannot make God unjust.

a: I am speaking as people do
p: Four objections, each answered: this is how an ancient teacher taught.
b: "I am speaking as people do" (kata anthropon) tells the reader that the thought is a human way of reasoning that Paul will reject. The four questions (3:1, 3, 5, 7) and the rejoinder in 3:8 follow the form of the ancient diatribe, a teaching style with an imagined partner, studied by Stowers and others. Whose objections are they? A Jewish opponent who thinks Paul's teaching makes God unjust (traditional reading); or Paul's own anticipation of what a Gentile or Jew might say after 2:1–29. Some scholars see here a reflection of real accusations made against Paul (3:8). In this verse the Plain writes "injustice" and "unjust" for adikia and adikos, because the charge is that God would be unfair. Elsewhere in this part the same Greek root is "unrighteousness" (1:18, 29; 2:8), and the Plain at 9:14 also says "unjust."

a: how will God judge the world
p: Paul's answer echoes Abraham's question to God about Sodom.
b: Abraham asked God about Sodom: "Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25). Paul takes for granted, as every Jewish reader did, that God is judge of the world; the only question is how his judgment can be just. The point of "By no means!" is that if God cannot judge sin, then he cannot judge the world at all. The answer is not given here; it comes in 3:21–26, where God shows how he can be righteous and still justify the sinner.

a: as we are slandered for saying
p: People accused Paul of teaching "let us do evil so that good may come."
b: Paul seems to have been accused of saying that sin is fine if grace results. The charge is mentioned again in 6:1, 15, and the book of Acts reports a rumor that Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses (Acts 21:21). These accusations may have reached Rome through traveling believers, and Paul wants to answer them before he arrives. It is the kind of risk his teaching on grace always ran: a message that says no one earns anything can be heard as a license. The rest of the letter (6:1–23; 12:1–15:13) answers it.

p: The Greek verb is rare and can be read three ways.
b: Proechometha is a rare verb. The middle voice could mean "do we have an advantage?" (the Plain). A passive reading, "are we at a disadvantage / are we excelled?", has been proposed; and a middle "do we shield ourselves?" (do we make a defense?) has its defenders. The first reading continues 3:1–2. The reply that follows, ou pantos, is also disputed: "not at all" (a strong denial) or "not in every way" (Paul keeps the advantage of 3:2 but denies that it gives any shelter). The Plain says "No, not in any way," a denial of the shelter. In either case the answer is that Jews and Greeks stand alike under sin. "Greeks" means here all non-Jews, as in 1:16 and 10:12.

p: In Romans sin is something that rules people, like a ruler, a power.
b: Paul writes "under sin" (hyph' hamartian), as one might say "under a ruler" or "under the law." Sin in Romans is less often a single wrong act than a power that holds humanity (5:12–21; 6:6, 14, 17–20; 7:8–11). The picture is of a world under occupation. Paul's phrase "Jews and Greeks alike" shows he means every human being. The Plain keeps "sin" in lowercase, as the term list asks, with the note that Paul speaks of it as a power.

p: Paul strings together six Old Testament passages, a practice Jewish teachers used.
b: Verses 10–18 are a chain, a "string of pearls" in the Jewish teaching style called charaz. The sources: Psalm 14:1–3 (= Psalm 53:1–3); Psalm 5:9; Psalm 140:3; Psalm 10:7; Isaiah 59:7–8; Psalm 36:1. The first line, "No one is righteous," is not exactly any one verse, but resembles Psalm 14 and Ecclesiastes 7:20: "there is no human being on the earth so righteous that he does good and does not sin" (Ecclesiastes 7:20). Paul follows the Greek Old Testament, which differs from the Hebrew in places. The Latin Vulgate and some Septuagint manuscripts carry the whole chain of Romans 3:13–18 inside Psalm 14, and most scholars think copyists added it from Romans.
r: Psalm 14:1–3; Psalm 5:9; Psalm 140:3; Psalm 10:7; Isaiah 59:7–8; Psalm 36:1; Ecclesiastes 7:20

p: The Psalm says God looks down to see whether anyone seeks him.
b: In Psalm 14 the LORD looks down from heaven to see "whether any seek God" (Psalm 14:2). Paul puts the result into one line: no one searches for God. The Psalm begins with the fool who says to himself that there is no God (Psalm 14:1), which echoes Paul's word for those who became fools in 1:22. The Psalm describes the "fool" and a sinful humanity but also speaks of a refuge for the poor and of God's people who are not part of the evildoers (Psalm 14:5–7); Paul does not quote that part here.

a: No one does good; there is not even one.
p: Paul's "not even one" repeats the Psalm's "not a single one."
b: The Plain of Psalm 14:3 reads: "No one does good, no, not a single one." The Greek Psalm uses a word for kindness or goodness; Paul's text has the same. In the Hebrew Psalm, the verdict is a description of the "fool" and the wicked of the day. By the time of Paul, readers took the verse as a statement about all humanity. Whether Paul means that every single person is without any good, or that no one is without sin before God (the point of 3:9, 19–20), is debated; most interpreters take it in the second sense.

p: From Psalm 5, which speaks of the enemies of the one who prays.
b: Psalm 5:9 in this site's Plain reads: "their throat is a grave left open" (Psalm 5:9). It describes the enemies of David, whose speech is false and deadly. Paul follows the Greek wording of the same line, "with their tongues they practiced deceit"; the clause is in the Hebrew too, where the Plain of Psalm 5:9 has "their tongues are slippery with flattery." Paul uses the whole body in his picture: throat, tongue, lips, mouth (3:13–14), feet (3:15–17), eyes (3:18). The chain of body parts is the picture of a person completely given over to sin.

a: The venom of snakes is under their lips.
p: Paul's Greek says "asps" (cobras). The Hebrew has "vipers."
b: The Plain of Psalm 140:3 reads: "under their lips lies the venom of the viper" (Psalm 140:3). The Greek Psalm has "asps," and Paul follows it. The picture is of speech that poisons. Like Psalm 5:9, the verse describes the speech of those who attack the righteous. Paul gives it a wider reach: it describes the speech of everyone before God.

a: Cursing and bitterness fill their mouths.
p: From a Psalm about the wicked man who thinks God does not see.
b: Psalm 10:7 in the Plain begins: "Cursing fills his mouth" (Psalm 10:7). The Psalm describes a wicked man who thinks God does not see. The Greek Psalm adds "bitterness" (its mouth "full of cursing and bitterness and deceit"), as in Paul. The chain moves from speech to violence in the next verses.

a: Their feet run fast to spill blood.
p: Paul uses Isaiah's picture of a people whose feet run toward evil.
b: Isaiah 59:7 in the Plain reads: "they hurry to shed innocent blood" (Isaiah 59:7). Isaiah 59 describes the sin of Israel and Judah that keeps God's salvation from them. It is a chapter about Israel's own failings, and Paul applies it to the whole world. In 11:26–27 he will quote the end of the same chapter (Isaiah 59:20–21), in which a redeemer comes to Zion. So Isaiah 59 holds both Paul's charge and his hope.

p: Isaiah 59:8 says Israel did not know the way of peace. Paul will speak of peace in 5:1.
b: The Plain of Isaiah 59:8 reads: "They do not know the way of peace" (Isaiah 59:8). Peace is a main theme of the next chapters: those justified by faith have peace with God (5:1), and the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace (8:6). Luke 1:79 speaks of steering our feet "onto the road of peace." The ruin described here is the problem the letter will solve.

p: The last line of the chain: no fear of God. It names the root of the rest.
b: Psalm 36:1 in the Plain reads: "He has no dread of God" (Psalm 36:1). The "fear of the LORD" is the beginning of wisdom in the Bible (Proverbs 9:10). The charge that opened in 1:21, that people did not honor God as God, closes here with the same idea. The chain began with "no one is righteous" and ends with the root cause, no fear of God.

p: The chain was addressed to Jews. Paul uses it to silence the whole world.
b: The Psalms and Isaiah are "the law" here in a wide sense, the whole Scripture. Paul says it speaks to "those who are inside the law" (tois en to nomo, "those in the law"), which means Jews. This is not the phrase "under the law" (hypo nomon) that he uses later (6:14–15); at 2:12 the same preposition is "inside the law." and that its purpose is to close every mouth. The logic: if the people who have the law are charged with the charges of the chain, then no Jew can claim immunity, and if the Jews are not exempt, then the Gentiles, whose case was made in 1:18–32, are not either. "Answerable" (hypodikos) means liable to judgment, "brought to trial." The rest of the letter will say the law cannot save, but it can show the situation.
orig: ὑπόδικος (hypodikos); τοῖς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ (tois en tō nomō)

p: Does Paul mean good deeds in general, or the Jewish marks of identity such as circumcision and food laws?
b: Paul writes erga nomou, "works of the law" (3:20, 28; Galatians 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10). Traditional (Reformation) reading: any deeds done to earn God's favor; no one can keep the law well enough (Luther; Moo, Schreiner). The New Perspective: the law's boundary markers of Jewish identity, circumcision, Sabbath and food laws, which kept Jews and Gentiles apart (Dunn, Wright, building on Sanders' picture of Judaism). Qumran: the Dead Sea text 4QMMT, "Some of the Works of the Torah," uses the Hebrew phrase for the specific rules its group required, which Dunn and Fitzmyer cite. Combined: some scholars hold these readings together, since the works are the law's requirements and function both as boundary marks and as an attempt at merit. Behind the debate: E. P. Sanders argued that Judaism of the time did not teach earning salvation by works, but that people enter by God's grace and stay by obedience. Many scholars have accepted that picture; others (Gathercole, Carson) hold that some Jewish texts expected vindication on the basis of obedience.

p: Paul echoes the Psalm and adds "by works of the law."
b: Psalm 143:2 in the Plain reads: "for no living person is in the right in your presence" (Psalm 143:2). The Greek Psalm also says "no one living." Paul writes "no flesh" (pasa sarx), his own wording: "flesh" here means a human being, weak and mortal, and the gloss says "no human being." The Plain keeps the site's one word "flesh" for sarx, so that Galatians 2:16 reads the same. Paul adds "by works of the law," a phrase not in the Psalm. The Psalm is a prayer by someone who throws himself on God's mercy, not on his own merit, and Paul hears in it the same plea.

t: The law gives knowledge of sin
p: The law shows sin for what it is. Paul says more about this in 4:15, 5:20 and 7:7–13.
b: Epignosis hamartias is a full recognition of sin. The law does not cure; it diagnoses. Later in the letter this is spelled out: the law brings anger (4:15), makes sin visible as a breach of a command (5:13), makes trespass increase (5:20), and shows through the commandment "You shall not covet" what sin is (7:7–13). None of this says the law is bad (7:12). It tells the truth about sin and so closes every mouth (3:19).

p: A turn in time: from the long indictment to what God has done.
b: Nyni de, "but now," marks the great hinge of the letter. It is not only a turn in the argument but a turn in time: what was hidden is now plain. Paul uses "now" at the other turns of the story: 3:26 ("the present time"), 5:9, 6:22, 7:6, 8:1, 11:30, 16:26. The verb "made plain" (phaneroo) is the verb of 1:19 (what God made plain about himself in creation), now used for his saving action. 3:21–26 is a dense paragraph, and many commentators call it the center of the letter.

a: God's righteousness has been made plain
p: Look back at 1:17. The readings are tested here: 3:25–26 says God's righteousness is shown by what he did.
b: At 1:17 the Plain listed four readings of God's righteousness (a gift, his justice, his covenant faithfulness, his saving power). Look at how Paul uses it here: God's righteousness is made plain and reaches all who believe (3:21–22), so it is something received; God puts Christ forward to show his righteousness (3:25–26), so it is also something God does and that vindicates his own character; and he is righteous himself while he justifies (3:26), so it includes God's own uprightness. Most commentators now say Paul's phrase holds more than one of these at once. Luther, looking back in the preface to his Latin works (1545), wrote that he had at first hated the phrase, and that when he saw it was a gift, all of Scripture showed him a different face and he felt he had entered paradise. That is his own late recollection, and historians disagree about when this "tower experience" took place.

a: the Law and the Prophets give witness to it
p: In this verse "law" is both what God's righteousness is apart from, and what bears witness to it.
b: "Apart from the law" means apart from the commandments as a way to be right with God. "The Law and the Prophets" means the Scriptures: the first five books and the prophetic books. So Paul says the new thing is not against the old. The witnesses he calls are chiefly Genesis 15:6 (chapter 4), Habakkuk 2:4 (1:17), Psalm 32:1–2 (4:7–8), and the sacrifice system and Isaiah 53, which lie behind 3:25. Jews and Christians have read this claim differently. For Paul the Scriptures speak of Christ; for Jewish readers the Law and the Prophets were already complete.
r: Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4; Psalm 32:1–2; Isaiah 53:11–12; Romans 4:3; Luke 24:44

t: "Faith in Jesus Christ" or "the faithfulness of Jesus Christ"
p: The Greek can mean our faith in Christ or Christ's own faithfulness. The question is debated; the Plain follows the majority reading.
b: The Greek is pistis Iesou Christou, "faith of Jesus Christ." Objective reading (our faith in him): most translations, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Moo, Cranfield. Subjective reading (Christ's own faithfulness): Richard Hays (The Faith of Jesus Christ), Wright in part, Douglas Campbell. For the subjective: the grammar of "faith of" most naturally names the one who has the faith; Paul says elsewhere "the faith of Abraham" (4:12, 16); the verse is not repetitive ("through faith ... to all who believe"); Christ's obedience is central in 5:19. For the objective: Paul's own statement that "we" believed in Christ Jesus (Galatians 2:16) and the emphasis on human faith throughout chapter 4. The same question arises at 3:26, Galatians 2:16, 3:22 and Philippians 3:9. The Plain follows the objective reading, the view of most translators and commentators, and the gloss gives the other.

p: The same phrase returns in 10:12.
b: Diastole, "distinction" or "difference," appears in Paul only in Romans 3:22 and 10:12, both times about Jew and Greek (its only other use in the New Testament is 1 Corinthians 14:7, of the distinct notes of an instrument). The first time it is about sin and righteousness (all sinned, all are offered the same righteousness); the second about the Lord of all. The phrase is the heart of Paul's argument that Jew and Gentile stand on the same ground, which he will use in the next verses and in chapter 4.

p: Paul says "all sinned" with a past-tense verb. See 5:12 for the question of Adam.
b: The verb hemarton is an aorist, a past-tense "sinned," which Paul uses again in 5:12 ("all sinned"). Readers disagree on whether it means each person's own sins, or the sin of humanity in Adam, or both. Paul's whole argument from 1:18 to 3:20 makes the first sense plain: Jews and Gentiles have each sinned. The second belongs to chapter 5, which is handled in the part of the Plain for chapters 5–8. The next phrase says what sin costs.

a: all lack the glory of God
p: "The glory of God" may mean the glory Adam had before he sinned.
b: The verb hystereo means to fall short of, to lack. "The glory of God" can mean God's approval or praise, the share in his radiance humanity was made for (Psalm 8:5), or the presence of God. Several Jewish writings speak of Adam losing a glory. The Qumran Community Rule (a Dead Sea scroll, in no church's Bible) says that the faithful will have all the glory of Adam (1QS 4:23), and in the Life of Adam and Eve (the Greek Apocalypse of Moses 20; a Jewish work that is in no church's Bible) Adam, after the fall, says he was stripped of the righteousness in which he was clothed. Paul's own thread: humans swapped God's glory for idols (1:21, 23), lack it (3:23), hope for it (5:2) and will share it (8:17–30). Dunn and others find Adam behind 3:23; Moo thinks the sense is wider.

p: Dorean means "as a gift, with nothing paid." The same root appears in 5:15–17.
b: Dorean is "freely," "as a gift," from dorea, a gift. Paul later says the free gift of righteousness comes through one man, Jesus Christ (5:15–17). The word underlines that no payment comes from the sinner. Paul says it again in 4:4–5: for the person who works, wages are a debt; for the one who trusts, the gift is grace. In the Roman world of favors and obligations, a gift with no return was surprising. John Barclay argues that Paul's idea of grace is unconditioned: it does not depend on the worth of the receiver, though it demands a changed life.

a: the redemption found in Christ Jesus
p: A word from the slave market and from the Exodus: being set free by a price paid.
b: Apolytrosis comes from lytron, a ransom or price paid for release. It was used for buying a slave or prisoner of war out of captivity. The Bible's own picture is the Exodus, when God "redeemed" Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8; 15:15), and Jesus says he came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Debated: whether the language of payment should be pressed. Some church fathers asked who was paid (Gregory of Nyssa suggested the devil); Anselm and later teachers said the debt was owed to God; others say the image means only liberation. See the card at 3:25.

p: The word may mean the lid of the ark, an offering that turns away anger, or one that removes sin.
b: Hilasterion appears in the Greek Old Testament for the "atonement lid" of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Exodus 25:17–22; Leviticus 16). "He must not come before the atonement lid on the ark, or he will die" (Leviticus 16:2). Hebrews 9:5 uses it that way. The atonement lid (Luther's Gnadenstuhl, "seat of grace"; Manson, Wright, Dunn): Christ is where God and sinners meet. Propitiation (turning away God's anger: Morris, Stott, Packer). Expiation (removing sin: Dodd). The martyr's death: 4 Maccabees 17:22 (a book printed in some Orthodox Bibles, and not Scripture for Catholics or Protestants) says the martyrs' death was an "atonement." The Plain uses the neutral "place of atonement," and the gloss says "where sin is covered over." No view is ranked here. See the card and the topic page on atonement.
r: Exodus 25:17–22; Leviticus 16:2; Leviticus 16:14–15; Hebrews 9:5; 4 Maccabees 17:22; Romans 5:9–11

p: Blood means a life given. The Greek word order links "faith" and "blood" in a way that can be read two ways.
b: The Plain says "through faith, by his blood." The Greek phrase dia pisteos en to autou haimati can be read "through faith in his blood" or "a place of atonement in his blood, received through faith." The Old Testament says, "a body's life is in its blood ... It is the blood that makes atonement, by means of the life in it" (Leviticus 17:11). Blood means life given up, not only death. Paul speaks of "his blood" again in 5:9. Readers differ on whether the blood stands for the sacrifice of the cross as a substitute, a cleansing of defilement, or a life offered to God that Christians share (Lutheran and Catholic traditions emphasize the Lord's Supper).

p: Paresis is not "forgiveness": it means letting sins go unpunished for a time.
b: Paresis ("passing over") is a rare word, found here only in the New Testament, and it differs from aphesis, "forgiveness." It means God held back from punishing earlier sins. Paul says God did this in his "forbearance" (anoche, as in 2:4). Acts 17:30 says something similar: God "overlooked" the times of ignorance. Paul's point is that holding back could look like injustice; the cross shows that God was not ignoring sin but waiting. The "sins done earlier" (progegonoton hamartematon) were those before Christ's death, either of the nations or of Israel under the old covenant (Hebrews 9:15 has a related idea).

a: he is righteous himself and that he justifies
p: God proves his own righteousness by justifying the one who has faith.
b: The Greek is dikaion kai dikaiounta, "righteous and justifying," a play on the same root. It answers the question of 3:3–5 (does God's righteousness stand if he lets sinners go?) and of 3:25 (how can he pass over sins?). The answer: God is shown to be righteous by justifying, because in the cross he deals with sin and keeps his promise at once. Readers differ on whether "justify" means "declare righteous" (the Reformation reading) or "make righteous" (Augustine and Catholic teaching); the Greek word is the same, and the churches' views are on the card.

p: The same question as 3:22. The Greek is ek pisteos Iesou.
b: Ton ek pisteos Iesou is literally "the one of Jesus' faith." The Plain reads "the one who has faith in Jesus." Those who read 3:22 subjectively would translate "the one who lives from the faithfulness of Jesus" (Hays, Campbell). The case for the objective reading here is that the phrase "the one from faith" is Paul's expression for any believer (4:16; Galatians 3:7, 9), and Jesus' name is the one believed. The note at 3:22 sets out the arguments.
orig: τὸν ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ (ton ek pisteōs Iēsou)

p: What was the boasting? Pride in one's own works, or pride in being Jewish?
b: Kauchesis, "boasting," has appeared in 2:17, 23. Readings: self-reliance on one's own moral record (Bultmann; the traditional reading). Ethnic pride that Jews are the people with the law and Gentiles are not (Dunn, Wright, the New Perspective). Confidence of final vindication before God (Gathercole, who argues from Jewish writings that many Jews expected to be vindicated by their obedience). The Old Testament approves boasting in the LORD (Jeremiah 9:24); Paul keeps that kind (5:11; 1 Corinthians 1:31). Boasting about oneself is "shut out" because the way of righteousness is a gift.
r: Romans 2:17; Romans 2:23; Romans 4:2; Romans 5:11; Jeremiah 9:24; 1 Corinthians 1:31

p: Paul uses "law" for a principle or rule, or for the Torah understood by faith.
b: Paul says "through the law of faith." Readers disagree on what "law" means. A rule or principle: the way of faith as a principle (Moo, Fitzmyer, and most translations: "the principle of faith"). The Torah itself, read in the light of faith (Cranfield, Wright), which would fit 3:31, where Paul says he upholds the law. The Plain keeps "law" so the reader sees that one word is used for both. The term list asks the Plain to say "law" and note the options.

p: The Greek says "by faith, apart from works of the law." Luther added "alone."
b: In his German New Testament (1522) Luther translated this verse as justified "by faith alone" (allein durch den Glauben). The Greek has no word for "alone." Catholic critics objected at once. In his Open Letter on Translating (1530) Luther defended the addition as good German idiom and as the clear sense of "apart from works of the law." Both sides can point to the Greek: it says "by faith" and it says "without works," so the teaching "faith alone" is, for Lutherans and Reformed, a fair statement of what Paul says; Catholic teaching accepts "by faith" but holds that faith does not stand alone (Council of Trent, session 6, chapters 8 and 9). The churches' positions are on the card.

a: Is God God for Jews alone?
p: Paul uses the Shema, "the LORD is one," to say that God is God of the Gentiles too.
b: "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the daily prayer of Jews. Paul uses the oneness of God to make the point that there cannot be one God for Jews and another for Gentiles. The prophets already said it: "Turn to me, all you ends of the earth, and be saved" (Isaiah 45:22), and Zechariah 14:9 promises that the LORD will be king over all the earth and "one." The argument is from within Jewish belief about God.

a: from faith, and the uncircumcised through that faith
p: Paul uses two different prepositions for the same faith. Does he mean a difference?
b: Paul says God justifies the circumcised "from faith" (ek pisteos) and the uncircumcised "through that faith" (dia tes pisteos, with the article, "the faith" just named). Some have found a difference; most say none, and that Paul varies the preposition for style. The point is that there is one God and one faith for both groups. The article "the" in the second phrase, "the same faith," makes the unity explicit.
orig: ἐκ πίστεως ... διὰ τῆς πίστεως (ek pisteōs ... dia tēs pisteōs)

p: Paul denies that faith cancels the law. He does not say how he upholds it.
b: Histanomen means to make stand, to establish. How? The proposals: faith confirms the law's witness to Christ (3:21); faith fulfills the law's goal, which is love (13:8–10), through the Spirit (8:4); faith recovers the law's true purpose, as chapter 4 does with Abraham; the law is established as the standard that exposes sin (3:20). In Jewish readings of Paul, this verse is evidence that Paul did not abandon the Torah for himself or for Jews (Nanos, Gager); other readings hold that he thought the law was no longer the believer's way (10:4, a question for the other parts). The Greek Fathers and Reformers both held that Christ and the Spirit fulfill the law.

a: our forefather according to the flesh
p: Paul calls Abraham "our" forefather, which includes Gentile believers, and "according to the flesh," which is Jewish descent.
b: Why Abraham? He was the model of a person made right with God, the father of the Jewish people, and, in Jewish tradition, the first person to know the one God. Abraham was also thought of as the father of converts. A Mishnah rule (Bikkurim 1:4) says a convert may bring first fruits but may not say the words "which the LORD swore to our fathers," since the patriarchs are not his fathers. A later Jewish teacher in the Jerusalem Talmud and Maimonides (in his letter to Obadiah the convert) held that a convert may say them, because Abraham is father of all who come to God. Paul takes the second view much further: Abraham is father of all who believe, Jew or Gentile (4:11–12, 16).

p: Many Jews of Paul's time read Genesis 15:6 as praise for Abraham's loyalty under testing.
b: Paul's opponents had a strong case from Jewish tradition. Sirach 44:20 (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians) says Abraham kept the law of the Most High and was found faithful when tested; 1 Maccabees 2:52 (likewise) asks whether Abraham was not found faithful in testing and so had it reckoned to him as righteousness; Jubilees 23:10 (Scripture only for the Ethiopian Orthodox church) praises him as perfect in righteousness all his life; and the Mishnah (Qiddushin 4:14) says he kept the whole Torah before it was given. Read this way, Genesis 15:6 rewards Abraham's obedience, especially at the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22). Paul reverses it: Genesis 15:6 comes before the testing, before circumcision (Genesis 17), and speaks of trust in a promise. James 2:21–24 takes the older view of Abraham, with a different meaning of "justified" (see the note at 4:3).

a: For what does the Scripture say?
p: James 2:21–24 quotes the same verse and says people are justified by works. The two letters mean different things.
b: James says Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac, and that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (James 2:21, 24).
