The apparent contradiction has been read many ways. Different senses: Paul uses "justify" for being declared right with God when one starts, and "works" for works of the law that mark membership; James uses "justify" for being shown right in the final judgment, and "works" for deeds of mercy that prove faith is alive. Different opponents: Paul fights the claim that Gentiles must keep the law; James fights a claim that faith needs no deeds. Luther found the two hard to reconcile and called James a "strawy" letter in 1522; Catholic and Orthodox teachers see them as two halves of one teaching; Reformed and Lutheran confessions say faith alone justifies but is never alone. See the card on faith and works below.

p: Paul quotes the key verse. It comes after Abraham complains that he has no child and God shows him the stars.
b: This site's Plain of the Hebrew reads: "Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). In Genesis 15 Abram is old, childless and afraid (Genesis 15:1–2), and God promises offspring as many as the stars: "So will your offspring be" (Genesis 15:5). Paul follows the Greek Bible, which turns the verb into a passive: "it was reckoned to him." In the Hebrew it is not clear who does the reckoning, God or Abram; Paul takes it as God's. The trust is in a promise about a child, and Paul reads it as trust in the God who gives life (4:17–21).

a: it was reckoned to him as righteousness
p: An accounting word. What is credited to Abraham, and does the churches' teaching on "imputation" come from it?
b: Logizomai is an account-book word: to count, credit, reckon. It occurs 11 times in chapter 4. The Hebrew chashab is used in the same way in Psalm 106:31, where Phinehas' zeal "was reckoned to him as righteousness" (Psalm 106:31), and the Qumran letter 4QMMT uses the same wording for those who do what the Torah requires. Readers differ on what is credited. Reformed and Lutheran: Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer, who is declared righteous (Calvin, Institutes 3.11). Catholic: God counts the person righteous because he makes him so by grace (Trent, session 6). New Perspective: Abraham is counted as a member of the covenant family (Wright). The Plain keeps the word "reckoned" to follow it through the chapter.

a: wages are not reckoned as a favor but as a debt
p: Paul uses the language of the Roman world of work and favors.
b: Paul's picture is the world of work and patronage. A wage is owed; a favor (charis, "grace") is given. He does not say that Jewish teachers thought of God as an employer. E. P. Sanders argued that most Jewish writers of the time believed God chose Israel by grace and asked for obedience to stay in the covenant ("covenantal nomism"). Many scholars have accepted this; others (Gathercole, Carson) think that some texts expected reward for obedience. John Barclay adds that the Jewish tradition spoke of grace as God's generous giving, but often linked to worth. Paul's argument here is the sharper one: if the reward were wages, grace would not be needed. Chapters 5–8 return to what grace does.

a: the One who justifies the ungodly
p: A judge who justifies the wicked is condemned in the Bible. Paul says God does this.
b: The Law told judges: "I will not count the wicked as righteous" (Exodus 23:7) and Proverbs 17:15 calls it abhorrent to the LORD to be "declaring the wicked innocent and declaring the righteous guilty" (Proverbs 17:15). Paul puts it in startling form: God is the One who "justifies the ungodly." The shock is intentional. He has already said that God must be shown righteous (3:25–26). The answer to the puzzle is that God does not simply ignore the wrong: he puts forward Christ's death as the place where it is dealt with (3:25), and the ungodly are not justified because they were good but because they trust.

a: David too speaks of the blessedness
t: David and Abraham tied by one word
p: Paul links Genesis 15:6 and Psalm 32 because both use the word "reckon." Jewish teachers used the same method.
b: Paul links two texts that share a key word, "reckon" (logizomai): Genesis 15:6 and Psalm 32:2 (the man whose sin the Lord will never reckon, 4:8). The rabbis called this method gezerah shavah, "equal category," and used it widely. The verb is the same in Hebrew and Greek: Hebrew chashab in Psalm 32:2 is the verb of Genesis 15:6, so the link works in Hebrew as well. The Plain of Genesis 15:6 renders it "reckoned," and the Plain of Psalm 32:2 renders it "charge": "Happy is the person the LORD does not charge with guilt" (Psalm 32:2). In English the link is hidden unless the reader sees that both are one verb. David is the king who sinned with Bathsheba and Uriah and confessed (Psalm 32 is traditionally linked to this; 2 Samuel 12:13). For Paul, the Psalm shows that the great sinner David too lives by God's refusal to count his sin.

p: "Covered" is the Hebrew word kapar, the root of atonement.
b: The Plain of Psalm 32:1 reads: "whose sin is covered over" . The Hebrew kasah (to cover) is a neighbor of kapar, the root of "atonement" (kippur), which gives the Day of Atonement and the atonement lid its name. In 3:25 Paul used the word for the atonement lid. The forgiven sins are covered, set out of sight before God, by what God himself provides.

a: Not when he was circumcised, but when he was uncircumcised.
t: The order of events in Genesis
p: Genesis 15 comes years before Genesis 17: faith first, circumcision after.
b: Paul argues from the order of the story. Abram's trust is reckoned as righteousness in Genesis 15:6. He is circumcised only in Genesis 17, when Abraham was ninety-nine: "Abraham was ninety-nine years old when the flesh of his foreskin was cut away" (Genesis 17:24). Ishmael was born when Abram was eighty-six (Genesis 16:16), and Genesis 15 comes before that, so at least thirteen years passed. Jewish teachers did not miss the point; they too noted that Abraham's righteousness came before the law and before circumcision, and some used this to say Abraham was a model for converts. Paul uses it to say circumcision is a seal, not a condition.

p: In later Christian writing baptism is also called a seal. Do the two rites correspond?
b: Genesis 17:11 calls circumcision "a sign" of the covenant; Paul adds that it was a "seal" (sphragis, a stamp that marks ownership or confirms a document). Later Christian writers called baptism a seal (2 Clement 7:6; Shepherd of Hermas, Similitudes 8.6.3; early Christian writings that are in no church's Bible). Whether baptism takes the place of circumcision is a question on which the churches disagree; the card on this verse gives four answers, and other churches answer in their own ways. Paul himself, in Colossians 2:11–12, links the two, and in Galatians he insists that Gentile believers need not be circumcised.
r: Genesis 17:11; Colossians 2:11–12; 2 Clement 7:6; Shepherd of Hermas, Similitudes 8.6.3

a: the father of every believer who is uncircumcised
p: Paul says Gentile believers are Abraham's children, with no need to become Jews.
b: The promise to Abraham was that he would be the father of a multitude of nations (Genesis 17:5). Paul draws the conclusion that those who share Abraham's faith are his children, circumcised or not. Readers differ on what this does to Gentiles. Traditional Christian: Gentile Christians become part of the people of Abraham, the "true Israel" or are grafted in. The "Paul within Judaism" reading (Fredriksen, Nanos, Gager): Gentiles stay Gentiles, and are included in the family of Abraham without being turned into Jews, so that Israel and the nations are distinct but joined. Both agree that Paul does not say Israel's own calling ends (11:29).

a: not just circumcised but also walk in the steps
p: Jewish believers are Abraham's children too, if they share his faith.
b: Paul adds that Abraham is also the father of the circumcised, with a condition: they must follow the steps of his faith. This is not a rejection of Jews; it is the prophets' demand (2:28–29, Jeremiah 9:25–26). In 3:3 Paul said that the unbelief of "some" does not cancel God's faithfulness, and in 11:1 he points to himself, a Jew who believes. Some read "those who walk" as Jewish Christians only; others as all circumcised people who trust God as Abraham did.

p: Genesis promises Abraham land. Jewish tradition and Paul enlarge it to the whole world.
b: Genesis promises Abraham's offspring a land (Genesis 12:7; 15:18) and, in 22:17–18, that the nations will be blessed through them. The phrase "heir of the world" is not in Genesis. Sirach 44:21 (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians) says God promised Abraham that his offspring would inherit from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth, and Jubilees 22 (Scripture only for the Ethiopian Orthodox church) has Abraham pray that his seed may inherit the whole earth (as reported in the commentaries). Paul takes the widening a step further. For him the promise reaches the whole created world (8:19–23), and Gentiles share in it (4:16). Whether he means the new creation, the nations, or a figure of speech for the land is debated.
r: Genesis 12:7; Genesis 15:18; Genesis 22:17–18; Sirach 44:21; Jubilees 22; Romans 8:19–23

p: Where there is a law, there is a line to cross. Paul does not say the law is bad.
b: "Transgression" (parabasis) is stepping across a marked line. Where no command exists, there is no crossing. This does not mean there was no sin before Moses; Paul says in 5:13 that sin was in the world before the law. The law "produces anger" because it names sin and makes it a breach of a known command (3:20; 7:7–13). The same word is used of Adam's sin in 5:14. The verse is part of Paul's argument that the promise could not be based on the law, since the law cannot give the inheritance, only the knowledge that it is lost.

a: I have made you the father of many nations.
p: "Nations" and "Gentiles" are the same Greek word.
b: The Plain of Genesis 17:5 reads: "I have made you father of a multitude of nations" (Genesis 17:5). Paul follows the Greek Old Testament: "father of many nations." The Greek word is ethne, the same word that means "Gentiles." So the verse reads two ways at once: Abraham is father of many nations, and father of the Gentiles. In Genesis, God changes Abram's name to Abraham, "father of a multitude" (Genesis 17:4–5), the verse Paul is using. God's "I have made you" is in the past tense, as if already done; that fits Paul's next phrase.

a: who makes the dead alive and calls the things that are not as though they were
p: Both phrases stand in Jewish prayer and teaching about God. Paul joins them to Abraham.
b: "Who makes the dead alive" is a description of God from the second blessing of the Jewish Amidah prayer, "who gives life to the dead" (mechayyeh hametim), a prayer whose present form is later than Paul, though the idea is much older. "Calls the things that are not" looks like creation out of nothing. The Plain of 2 Maccabees 7:28 (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians) says God made the world and human beings "not from things that were" (2 Maccabees 7:28), a Jewish writing before Paul. Hebrews 11:19 says Abraham expected God to raise Isaac. Paul sees both acts as one: the God who creates and raises is the God Abraham trusted to give a child to old bodies.

a: Against hope, he believed in hope
p: A paradox: against all human hope, in hope grounded in God's word.
b: The line sets two kinds of hope side by side. "Against hope" means that, humanly speaking, there was no ground for hope: Abraham and Sarah were beyond the age of children. "In hope" means a hope based on God's promise. Paul uses hope in the next chapter (5:2–5) and chapter 8 (8:24–25) in the same way. The quotation, "So will your offspring be," is from Genesis 15:5: "Look toward the sky and number the stars, if you can number them" (Genesis 15:5). The promise is in plain sight: the stars.

p: Genesis tells that Abraham laughed and that Sarah laughed. Paul tells a story without doubt.
b: Genesis does not present Abraham as free of doubt. After the promise of a son, "Abraham fell on his face and laughed" (Genesis 17:17), asking whether a man of a hundred could have a child. Sarah laughs too (Genesis 18:12), and earlier Abram took Hagar (Genesis 16). Paul does not mention any of this. Possible reasons: his point is Abraham's settled trust (4:20), as Jewish writers such as Philo also tidied Abraham's story; or Paul has in mind Abraham's attitude overall, and the laugh of Genesis 17:17 can be read as the laugh of joy. The text of this verse has a variant; see the entry on 4:19.

p: Abraham gives God the glory that the idolaters refused.
b: In 1:21 humanity knew God but "did not praise him as God." Here Abraham, with nothing to go on, "gave glory to God." Commentators such as N. T. Wright point out the pattern: Paul presents Abraham as the answer to Adam's family, a person who gives God the honor that others refuse. The two places share a root: 1:21 has the verb edoxasan ("they praised"), and 4:20 has the noun, dous doxan ("giving glory"); the glory of 1:23 and 3:23 is the same noun. Later in the letter the glory that was lost is promised again to those who suffer with Christ (8:17–30). The echo is a literary clue; Paul does not point it out.
orig: δοὺς δόξαν τῷ θεῷ (dous doxan tō theō)

a: who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead
p: The content of Christian faith is that God raised Jesus. Paul says it is the same trust as Abraham's.
b: Paul ends the chapter by saying that Genesis 15:6 was written "for ours too" and that the faith is in the God who raised Jesus. This is the earliest form of Christian confession: in 10:9 Paul says that faith includes believing that God raised Jesus from the dead. Abraham trusted the God who gives life to what is dead; Christians trust the God who has done it in Jesus. Hebrews 11:17–19 makes the same link from the other side. Some read Paul's line as a creed (1:3–4; 4:24–25), and 4:25 as one more fragment of it.

p: The wording follows the Greek of the Suffering Servant: "handed over for their sins."
b: The Greek Isaiah 53:12 says the servant "was handed over for their sins" (paredothe dia tas hamartias auton), words almost the same as Paul's. This site's Plain of the Hebrew reads: "He bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12). "Handed over" is also the verb of 1:24, 26, 28, where God hands humanity over to its sin, and of 8:32, where God hands over his own Son. The same word links the three: the Son is handed over into the place where humanity was handed over. Whether Paul has Isaiah 53 in view is debated (the verb is not rare), but the match in wording is close.
orig: παρεδόθη διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα (paredothē dia ta paraptomata)

p: Does Paul give the cross one job and the resurrection another?
b: The two clauses of 4:25 balance each other: handed over for trespasses, raised for justification. Does the cross deal with sin and the resurrection bring justification? Calvin read the two lines as covering the whole work of Christ between them, not as dividing it (commentary on Romans 4:25). Many modern commentators agree that the parallel is a pair of balanced lines, not a division of labor. Others hold that the resurrection is the confirmation of the verdict. The word dikaiosis ("justification") appears only here and in 5:18 in the New Testament.
